{{Short description|Mathematical notation}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Iverson bracket''', named after [[Kenneth E. Iverson]]<!-- mentioned here so it's clear that it's an upper-case 'i' not an 'l'. -->, is a notation that generalises the [[Kronecker delta]], which is the Iverson bracket of the statement {{math|1=''x'' = ''y''}}. It maps any [[statement (logic)|statement]] to a [[function (mathematics)|function]] of the [[free variable]]s in that statement. This function is defined to take the value 1 for the values of the variables for which the statement is true, and takes the value 0 otherwise. It is generally denoted by putting the statement inside square brackets:
<math display="block">[P] = \begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } P \text{ is true;} \\
0 & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}</math>
In other words, the Iverson bracket of a statement is the [[indicator function]] of the set of values for which the statement is true.

The Iverson bracket allows using [[capital-sigma notation]] without restriction on the summation index. That is, for any property <math>P(k)</math> of the integer <math>k</math>, one can rewrite the restricted sum <math>\sum_{k : P(k)}f(k)</math> in the unrestricted form <math>\sum_k f(k) \cdot[P(k)]</math>.  With this convention, <math>f(k)</math> does not need to be defined for the values of {{mvar|k}} for which the Iverson bracket equals {{math|0}}; that is, a summand <math>f(k)[\textbf{false}]</math> must evaluate to 0 regardless of whether <math>f(k)</math> is defined.

The notation was originally introduced by [[Kenneth E. Iverson]] in his programming language [[APL (programming language)|APL]],<ref name=APL>{{cite book|author=Kenneth E. Iverson|date=1962|title=A Programming Language|page=11 | publisher=Wiley |url=https://www.jsoftware.com/papers/APL.htm|access-date=7 April 2016}}</ref><ref>[[Ronald Graham]], [[Donald Knuth]], and [[Oren Patashnik]]. ''[[Concrete Mathematics]]'', Section 2.1: Notation.</ref> though restricted to single relational operators enclosed in parentheses, while the generalisation to arbitrary statements,  notational restriction to square brackets, and applications to summation, was advocated by [[Donald Knuth]] to avoid ambiguity in parenthesized logical expressions.<ref name=TNN>Donald Knuth, "Two Notes on Notation", ''[[American Mathematical Monthly]]'', Volume 99, Number 5, May 1992, pp.&nbsp;403–422. ([http://www-cs-faculty.stanford.edu/~knuth/papers/tnn.tex.gz TeX] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210506142926/http://www-cs-faculty.stanford.edu/~knuth/papers/tnn.tex.gz |date=2021-05-06 }}, {{arxiv|math/9205211}}).</ref>

==Properties==
There is a direct correspondence between arithmetic involving Iverson brackets, logical expressions, and set operations. For instance, let ''A'' and ''B'' be sets, and let <math>P(k_1,\dots)</math> and <math>Q(k_1,\dots)</math> be  properties of integers; then we have
<!--the [] directly after \begin{align} necessary because of how TeX handles arguments -->
<math display="block">\begin{align}[]
                       [\,P \land Q\,] ~ &= ~ [\,P\,]\,[\,Q\,]~~; \\[1em]
                        [\,P \lor Q\,] ~ &= ~ [\,P\,] \; + \; [\,Q\,] \; - \; [\,P\,]\,[\,Q\,]~~; \\[1em]
                        [\,\neg \,P\,] ~ &= ~ 1 - [\,P\,]~~; \\[1em]
[\,P {\scriptstyle\mathsf\text{ XOR }} Q\,] ~ &= ~ \Bigl|\,[\,P\,] \; - \; [\,Q\,] \, \Bigr| = ([P]-[Q])^2~~; \\[1em]
   [\,k \in A\,] \; + \; [\,k \in B\,] ~ &= ~ [\,k \in A \cup B\,] \; + \; [\,k \in A \cap B\,]~~; \\[1em]
                  [\,x \in A \cap B\,] ~ &= ~ [\,x \in A\,]\, [\,x \in B\,]~~; \\[1em]
       [\,\forall \,m\ : \, P(k, m)\,] ~ &= ~ \prod_m\, [\,P(k, m)\,]~~; \\[1em]
       [\,\exists \,m\ : \, P(k, m)\,] ~ &= ~ \min\Bigl\{\;1\,, \,\sum_m \,[\,P(k, m)\,]\;\Bigr\} = 1 \; -  \;\prod_m \, [\,\neg\, P(k, m)\,] ~~; \\[1em]
\#\Bigl\{\; m \,\Big| \, P(k, m)\;\Bigr\} ~ &= ~ \sum_m \, [\,P(k, m)\,]~~.
\end{align}</math>

==Examples==
The notation allows moving boundary conditions of summations (or integrals) as a separate factor into the summand, freeing up space around the summation operator, but more importantly allowing it to be manipulated algebraically.

===Double-counting rule===
<!-- is there a better name for this ? might be confused with combinatorics... -->
We mechanically derive a well-known sum manipulation rule using Iverson brackets:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\sum_{k\in A}f(k)+\sum_{k\in B}f(k)
&=\sum_kf(k)\,[k\in A]+\sum_kf(k)\,[k\in B]\\
&=\sum_kf(k)\,([k\in A]+[k\in B])
\\&=\sum_kf(k)\,([k\in A\cup B]+[k\in A\cap B])
\\&=\sum_{k\in A\cup
B}f(k)\ +\sum_{k\in A\cap B}f(k).
\end{align}</math>

===Summation interchange===
The well-known rule <math display="inline">\sum_{j=1}^n \sum_{k=1}^j f(j,k) = \sum_{k=1}^n \sum_{j=k}^n f(j,k)</math> is likewise easily derived:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\sum_{j=1}^n\,\sum_{k=1}^j f(j,k)
  &=\sum_{j,k}f(j,k)\,[1\leq j\leq n]\,[1\leq k\leq j]
\\&=\sum_{j,k}f(j,k)\,[1\leq k\leq j\leq n]
\\&=\sum_{j,k}f(j,k)\,[1\leq k\leq n]\,[k\leq j\leq n]

\\&=\sum_{k=1}^n\,\sum_{j=k}^n f(j,k).
\end{align}</math>

===Counting===
For instance, [[Euler's totient function]] that counts the number of positive integers up to ''n'' which are [[coprime]] to ''n'' can be expressed by
<math display="block"> \varphi(n)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\gcd(i,n)=1],\qquad\text{for } n\in\N^+.</math>

===Simplification of special cases===
Another use of the Iverson bracket is to simplify equations with special cases. For example, the formula
<math display="block">\sum_{1\le k\le n \atop \gcd(k,n)=1}\!\!k = \frac{1}{2}n\varphi(n)</math>

is valid for {{math|''n'' &gt; 1}} but is off by {{sfrac|1|2}} for {{math|1=''n'' = 1}}. To get an identity valid for all positive integers {{mvar|n}} (i.e., all values for which <math>\varphi(n)</math> is defined), a correction term involving the Iverson bracket may be added:
<math display="block">\sum_{1\le k\le n \atop \gcd(k,n)=1}\!\!k = \frac{1}{2}n \Big(\varphi(n)+[n=1]\Big)</math>

===Common functions===

Many common functions, especially those with a natural [[piecewise]] definition, may be expressed in terms of the Iverson bracket.  The [[Kronecker delta]] notation is a specific case of Iverson notation when the condition is equality. That is,
<math display="block">\delta_{ij} = [i=j].</math>

The [[indicator function]] of a set <math>A</math>, often denoted <math>\mathbf{1}_A(x)</math>, <math>\mathbf{I}_A(x)</math> or <math>\chi_A(x)</math>, is an Iverson bracket with set membership as its condition:
<math display="block">\mathbf{I}_A(x) = [x\in A].</math>

The [[Heaviside step function]], [[sign function]],<ref name=APL/> and [[absolute value]] function are also easily expressed in this notation:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
     H(x) &= [x \ge 0], \\
  \sgn(x) &= [x > 0] - [x < 0],
\end{align}</math>

and
<math display="block">\begin{align}
  |x| &= x[x > 0] - x[x < 0] \\
      &= x([x > 0] - [x < 0]) \\
      &= x \cdot \sgn(x).
\end{align}</math>

The comparison functions max and min (returning the larger or smaller of two arguments) may be written as
<math display="block">\max(x, y) = x[x > y] + y[x \leq y]</math> and
<math display="block">\min(x, y) = x[x \leq y] + y[x > y].</math>

The [[floor and ceiling functions]] can be expressed as
<math display="block">\lfloor x \rfloor = \sum_n n \cdot [n \le x < n + 1]</math>
and
<math display="block">\lceil x \rceil = \sum_n n \cdot [n - 1 < x \le n],</math>
where the index <math>n</math> of summation is understood to range over all the integers.

The [[ramp function]] can be expressed
<math display="block">R(x) = x \cdot [x \geq 0].</math>

The [[trichotomy (mathematics)|trichotomy]] of the reals is equivalent to the following identity:
<math display="block">[a < b] + [a = b] + [a > b] = 1. </math>

The [[Möbius function]] has the property (and can be defined by recurrence as<ref>[[Ronald Graham]], [[Donald Knuth]], and [[Oren Patashnik]]. ''[[Concrete Mathematics]]'', Section 4.9: Phi and Mu.</ref>)
<math display="block">\sum_{d|n} \mu(d)  =  [n=1],</math> where <math>d|n</math> means the sum is taken over all positive integers <math>d</math> that are divisors of <math>n</math>.

==Formulation in terms of usual functions==
In the 1830s, [[Guglielmo Libri Carucci dalla Sommaja|Guglielmo dalla Sommaja]] used the expression <math>0^{0^x}</math> to represent what now would be written <math>[x > 0]</math>; he also used variants, such as <math>\left(1 - 0^{0^{-x}}\right) \left(1 - 0^{0^{x-a}}\right)</math> for <math>[0 \leq x \leq a]</math>.<ref name=TNN/>
Following one [[zero to the power of zero|common convention]] (that <math>0^0=1</math>), those quantities are equal where defined: <math>0^{0^x}</math> is 1 if {{math|''x'' > 0}}, is 0 if {{math|1=''x'' = 0}}, and is undefined otherwise.

==Notational variations==
In addition to the now-standard square brackets {{nobr| [ · ] ,}} and the original parentheses {{nobr| (  ·  ) ,}} [[blackboard bold]] brackets have also been used, e.g. {{nobr| {{math| ⟦ · ⟧ }} ,}} as well as other unusual forms of bracketing marks available in the publisher's typeface, accompanied by a marginal note.
